newsitem.title: JAPAN: SOCCER-SUN SETS ON LONE ENGLISH J-LEAGUE BOSS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SUN SETS ON LONE ENGLISH J-LEAGUE BOSS.

text.p: Soccer manager Stuart Baxter is little known in his native England and barely remembered in Scotland where he spent his playing days.
However in Scandinavia he has plenty of admirers, while in Japan he is something of a hero for his efforts after an earthquake almost closed his club.

Baxter, boss of J-League team Vissel Kobe, is the only English manager in Japan's fledgling professional league -- but it is a distinction he is likely to relinquish this year as he has decided to move back to Europe.
Baxter says there have already been a number of enquiries for his services, including from clubs in Spain and Switzerland, and he has not ruled out a job in England under certain conditions.
"I know a lot of well-respected coaches in England like Arsene Wenger, Kenny Dalglish and Roy Evans and I think I've got a little bit of respect from the people I know," he says.
"To be fair to myself and to my family if I went back it would have to be a good club with ambitions. A club that wanted to go a different way because I don't think I'm typically British."
Baxter, whose father Bill played for Wolves and Aston Villa, was born in Birmingham. But he grew up in Scotland and played as a defender at Dundee United.
He made his name as a manager in Sweden where he took over as coach from the current Blackburn manager Roy Hodgson, formerly coach of the Swiss national team and Italy's Internazionale, at Oerbro.
He then guided Halmstads to promotion.
Baxter has been relatively successful in Japan with Sanfrecce Hiroshima, leading them to a first stage J-League title before joining Vissel Kobe and steering them into the J-League.
He was widely tipped to join Arsenal as the number two to Arsene Wenger at the beginning of last season but decided to stay in Japan for another J-League campaign with Kobe.

Baxter has strong emotional ties to the city and the club, having helped Vissel to recover from the devastation of the Great Hanshin Earthquake which struck Kobe in January 1995, killing 5,000 people and leaving 300,000 homeless.
The club was ready to join the J-League when the earth moved in Kobe.
Their main sponsor, Osaka-based supermarket chain Daiei, suffered huge losses from the quake and pulled out. The money Baxter was promised for team building was gone.
After the disaster Vissel Kobe's stadium was used as a refugee camp with helicopters carrying the homeless and injured in and out of the ground for days.
"Nobody who wasn't around during the earthquake can really understand it," says Baxter, who was scouting in Europe when the disaster happened. "It was an unbelievable tragedy."
Vissel were just hours away from liquidation but somehow survived.
"We had nowhere to train," recalls Baxter. "We were travelling two hours to a place with no showers and a big split up the middle where the earthquake had ripped through it."
The mayor of Kobe called Baxter and pleaded with him not to let Vissel go under. After losing the first nine games of the new season, Baxter gradually turned things around.
After signing Danish international Michael Laudrup, the club won promotion.
Today they are holding their own in the J-League, though Laudrup has since left to join Ajax of Amsterdam. Baxter expects to follow him home shortly.
